units.translation: In the Viennese Lexicon p. 95, 10, where see Nauck and in the Preface p. XLVIII. In Isocrates p. 351c, where now ἵππων ζεύγει is read, Naber restored τεθρίππῳ.
the strong yoke of the Atreidae
having cast such a yoke around Troy
father Theoinus, yoker of the Maenads
With the oblique cases Διός Διί Δία and the poetic forms Ζηνός Ζηνί Ζῆνα, which the tragedians do not use except when the meter demands.
where one should write Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινά, as I showed under δεσπόζω.
Ζηνός is to be restored for Διός when the meter demands.
where Pausanias 2, 24, 4 mentions Δία τὸν ἐν θαλάσση from Aeschylus, so that we do not know which case Aeschylus used.
In the denominative and vocative Ζήν
and one must expect that someone will be lord of Zeus
he sailed on the breeze of the giant Zephyrus
Thus I corrected for ὀργῆς νοσούσης, about which will be said under ὀργή.
words are healers of boiling anger
I deem you happy because you are free from blame
now I deem you happy in death, before seeing the depth of evils
being deemed happy, you led a blessed life among the Persians like a god
a penalty is attached to vain speech
in eagerness and daring, what penalty do you see present?
raging with penalties that deprive of wealth
and having passed over -- I will not speak the penalty
and do not seek to learn your own toils
In these three places in the books Zwá and ζωῆς are written in the manuscripts, a form which the tragedians did not use, as was said in the Thesaurus vol. 4 p. 55 after Elmsley on Eur. Med. 946.
and in the earth defiled with blood life is mingled
for bitter are the vapors and not of life
death is easier than a wretched life
under the darkness of the earth
Triclinius interpolated πραθέντα τλῆναι καὶ ζυγῶν θιγεῖν βία for π. τλήναι δουλίας μάζης βία, where Enger rightly has δουλίας μάζης τυχεῖν.
and I first yoked beasts under the yoke
he breaks the middle of the yoke
yielding to this necessity, make new the yoke
your entire yoke of the balance
never to hold the city of Cadmus with slavish yokes
to keep the slavish yoke away from this city
this city has escaped the slavish yoke
to cast a slavish yoke upon Hellas
having cast a yoke upon the neck of the sea
the yoke of strength was loosed
for no one willingly uses a slavish yoke
for one must bear the slavish yoke
when those in power are under the yoke of the spear
δαμάσω, κλείσω, καθέξω. Aeschylus in Circe the satyr play (fr. 113).
